paragraphs: The Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia, whose star chief executive Jensen Huang recently resigned after revelations of extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy and another with an employee, according to people familiar with the matter.

The civil investigation adds to the crisis facing Nvidia, whose shares have fallen more than 10% since Huang was ousted. The focus of the investigation couldn’t immediately be learned but includes whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, some of the people said,

Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected third quarter and a bullish outlook in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly spawned an SEC investigation.

On the company's earnings call, newly appointed chairman Harvey Jones said the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," despite a movement among some employees and investors to bring him back.
Why it matters: Nvidia remains squarely at the center of the AI economy — and investors are anxious for guidance on the company's strategic roadmap following Huang's sudden exit.
Zoom in: Nvidia recorded quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than doubling its performance from a year earlier.
S&P Capital IQ analysts had expected revenue of $108.7 billion and net income of $60.5 billion.
The company's data center revenue — its largest segment — rose 110% from a year ago to $107.6 billion.
The showing — which included a whopping gross profit margin of 74.8% — immediately calmed investors who have shaved more than $1 trillion off of Nvidia's market cap since the Huang scandal broke.
The stock was up as much as 5% in after-hours trading Tuesday following the company's earnings call.
It marks the first moment for interim CEO Colette Kress — who is also still serving as CFO — to exert her leadership during the most tumultuous moment in the company's history.
On the earnings call, she struck a steady tone, saying the company's momentum and innovation remain substantial.
Kress didn't mention Huang by name on the call but acknowledged the turbulent time and the "diverse" opinions — an apparent reference to the campaign to bring back Huang.
What we're watching: WSJ reported Tuesday afternoon that the SEC has opened a civil probe into the company.
An SEC spokesperson declined to comment.
Nvidia reps did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and the executives didn't discuss it on the call — but they said their quarterly 10Q filing with the SEC will be delayed.
The earnings call came hours after Huang posted a public letter saying he'd be "honored" to return as CEO.
Tech analyst Dan Ives earlier said the board could face a special shareholder meeting called by at least 15% of shareholders.

Jones said the company would not take questions on Huang's exit. He said the board would consider external and internal candidates and wants to move "as quickly as possible" but won't make a move until it finds "exactly the right person."
The intrigue: Huang reportedly faced pushback from Kress as he pushed financing deals to backstop the AI ecosystem.
On Tuesday's call, Kress signaled that the company would continue to provide financing where appropriate but would be "selective" and ensure that guarantees are necessary.
Editor's note: This story was updated to include comments from Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones and interim CEO Colette Kress made on the company's earnings call.

paragraphs: Jensen Huang is willing to return to Nvidia as chief executive should he be asked by directors to do so, the former CEO of the tech giant said Tuesday morning in his first public remarks since stepping down.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Jensen Huang said on Tuesday that he will come back as chief executive of Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) if the company's board wants him. It is the first time he has spoken publicly about a return since he resigned on Thursday, November 12.

The statement is five sentences long. Huang opened with an apology. He said he did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia and that he created problems for the board that he deeply regrets.
“I own my mistakes completely,” he said.

He then said he has seen calls for his return from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners and customers since he left. He did not ask for the job back. He left the decision to the directors.

As of Monday the board was not looking at a return. CNBC reported that directors are not considering bringing Huang back and are focused on their investigation of him, citing one person familiar with the matter. We covered that report this morning. Nvidia has not said on the record that a return is ruled out, and it had not responded publicly to Huang's statement when this story was published.

Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director after 33 years running the company he co-founded. CNBC reported that the board hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to examine his conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets. That review is still open.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim chief executive. Harvey C. Jones became the first board chair in Nvidia's history. A board representative said on Friday that the company was still choosing a search firm for a permanent chief executive.

An online petition asking the board to reinstate Huang had about 180,000 signatures on Monday, according to CNBC. Elon Musk, Y Combinator chief executive Garry Tan and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney are among the names on it. Two large shareholders, Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management, sent the board a letter asking it to move slowly and keep every option open, including Huang's return. We reported on the letter and the employees who signed the petition on Saturday.
President Trump was asked on Monday about Huang coming back. “I would certainly not mind seeing that,” he said.
Huang is also due in Washington. Reuters reported on Tuesday that he will appear before congressional committees in December.

Nvidia closed at $156.14 on Monday, its lowest close since July 1, 2025 and 34.7% below the record close of $239.24 set on October 6. At 10:54 a.m. ET on Tuesday, minutes before the statement, the shares were at $150.58, down 3.6% for the day and 37.1% below the record. By 11:04 a.m., after the statement, they had risen 2.5% to $154.38, down 1.1% for the day and 35.5% below the record.

The timing is hard to miss. Nvidia reports third-quarter results after the market closes on Tuesday, and Kress will lead the call. Analysts expect earnings of $2.47 a share on revenue of $109.15 billion. Nvidia's own forecast was $108.0 billion.

Boards have reversed themselves before. Steve Jobs went back to Apple in 1997, and $10,000 of Apple stock bought then grew to $18.6 million, as we reported on Sunday. The record for chief executives who are pushed out is less kind, and we looked at a study of 187 forced exits the day after Huang resigned.
The next move belongs to Nvidia's directors. They can answer Huang before tonight's earnings call, during it, or wait for the Wachtell review to finish.

paragraphs: By Leo Marchandon and Toby Sterling

Nov 17 (Reuters) – French robotics startup Genesis AI has raised $500 million in a funding round valuing it at $3.5 billion, the company said on Tuesday, one of the biggest funding rounds in Europe’s robotics sector as investors bet on demand for AI-enabled factory robots.

1027 ET - Oil futures pick up from the previous day's losses as shipping risks in the Middle East limit declines on expectations of a return to a global oil surplus. "More threats from Iran are being noted supporting crude futures in the early trade. However, lately they seem to be losing leverage," Dennis Kissler of BOK Financial says in a note. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

Nymex natural gas is down 2% at $3.06/mmBtu, retreating for a third consecutive session. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)
Gold Remains Pressured by Fed Rate-Hike Bets -- Market Talk

0906 GMT - Gold prices hold below $3,900 a troy ounce, pressured by expectations of a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike next month. "Sentiment remains fragile, with rising Fed rate-hike expectations and a firmer dollar outweighing support from falling energy prices," analysts at Saxo Bank say. "This divergence highlights concerns that inflationary pressures are becoming broader, stickier and more difficult to reverse." Investors now await the release of the Fed's October meeting minutes for more cues on the monetary policy outlook. In early European trading, gold futures rise 0.4% to $3,869 an ounce. Meanwhile, silver rises 1.2% to $47.45 an ounce and platinum is up 0.6% at $1,457.30 an ounce. (giulia.petroni@wsj.com)

0859 GMT - Gold prices are expected to remain well above pre-Covid levels in the coming years, hovering around $4,000 a troy ounce, according to BMI. The outlook, however, is subject to risks in both directions, with geopolitical developments and shifts in U.S. monetary policy likely to shape the metal's trajectory. A preliminary deal to end the U.S.-Iran conflict could ease oil prices and inflationary pressures, paving the way for earlier Federal Reserve rate cuts. A weaker dollar would provide further support, potentially lifting prices back above $4,500 an ounce, analysts at the firm say. But a renewed escalation in the conflict, or a sharper rise in the dollar and bond yields if the Fed resumes raising rates, could undermine demand. Higher yields would make non-interest-bearing gold less attractive, potentially triggering a selloff that pushes prices back to the $3,000-$3,500 range, BMI says. (giulia.petroni@wsj.com)

paragraphs: Governments and national cyber agencies protect the systems that people, public services and economies depend on. Through Daybreak, we’re putting advanced AI into the hands of trusted defenders for authorized security work, from reviewing software and investigating suspicious activity to validating vulnerabilities, and developing and testing fixes.

OpenAI works with NATO’s Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) to provide NATO’s core institutions with access to advanced cybersecurity models, helping protect Allied networks. NATO has used up to 300 billion raw input and output tokens per month as part of this work.

NATO’s early use of OpenAI tools shows how capable cyber defenders can put frontier models to work, supporting NATO’s mission of safeguarding the freedom and security of its member states. It also helps strengthen cyber expertise across multinational teams responsible for protecting Allied networks around the clock, and creates lessons that can benefit defenders across Europe and the broader Alliance.

OpenAI also supported (opens in a new window) the 2026 Crossed Swords exercise. Organized by the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE), the exercise included a new training stream in which participants built, deployed, and evaluated AI agents for cyber operations, using OpenAI Daybreak in the technical environment. The training put participants alongside AI agents as operators, with an emphasis on maintaining human oversight.
OpenAI remains fully committed to NATO’s principles for responsible AI adoption and to delivering solutions that are safe and secure.
Beyond NATO, we have already provided access to our cyber models to defenders in Europe, including the EU’s ENISA and national cyber agencies in France (ANSSI), Germany and Poland.

The Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine is using OpenAI’s Daybreak tool to strengthen the cyber defence of civilian infrastructure. The initiative is designed to help Ukrainian teams identify software vulnerabilities and develop and test fixes more quickly, supporting defenders who protect essential services amid persistent cyber attacks.

The EU’s cyber agency, ENISA, used our models to identify four vulnerabilities in software used across EU institutions, with fixes published for all four (1 (opens in a new window), (opens in a new window)2 (opens in a new window), (opens in a new window)3 (opens in a new window), (opens in a new window)4 (opens in a new window)). A November (opens in a new window)joint report from ENISA and CERT-EU (opens in a new window) also describes a review of 27 software projects using frontier models including OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak, and tools including the Codex security plug-in. Across the models tested, 95% of the 88 potential issues assessed by software maintainers were confirmed as genuine, demonstrating the value of combining AI with human expertise.

CERT Polska used OpenAI models to help identify six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS (opens in a new window) and coordinated their disclosure with the vendor. Researchers directed the work, tested findings on real systems and verified their impact, with AI accelerating analysis and the exploration of potential vulnerabilities. MikroTik released fixes, which CERT Polska confirmed prevented the attacks it had observed, giving network operators a concrete way to protect affected devices.

We will continue working with governments, national cyber agencies and international partners to turn frontier AI capability into stronger, safer, more resilient systems, helping defenders find weaknesses, fix them faster and protect the services people rely on every day.

paragraphs: Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, operated on two tracks pointed at the same goal of vaulting China’s artificial-intelligence capabilities ahead of the U.S.

Her job: cultivating a relationship—one that turned romantic—with Nvidia’s then-CEO Jensen Huang and securing a pipeline of the company’s advanced-computing chips that Washington has sought to keep from China. His job: building a sprawling network of government-backed data centers across China, a review of Chinese public records shows.
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Kang Wei, the husband of suspected spy and ex-Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, ran an extensive Beijing-backed AI data center empire in China – even as she carried on an affair with disgraced Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, according to a report Monday.

The couple – now at the center of a widening national security scandal that forced Jensen Huang to resign – worked together on efforts to help China erase America’s lead in the AI race, the Wall Street Journal reported. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang — also known as Huang Le — have no relation.
Kang secured investments worth more than $9 billion from 2021 to 2024 as part of a government-backed push to build out AI infrastructure in China.
In a bizarre twist, Kang has told people that he introduced his wife to Jensen Huang and even seemed to accept that they were romantically involved, according to the Journal.

Meanwhile, US officials have raised concerns that Alice Huang’s Megaspeed, which operated data centers in Singapore, was smuggling Nvidia-made AI chips to China in violation of US export controls. Megaspeed has strongly denied wrongdoing and claims Alice Huang is no longer employed by the company.

The Journal said its review of public records, including securities filings and government announcements in China, did not include definitive evidence linking the Chinese government to Megaspeed’s pipeline of Nvidia chips or signs that those chips ultimately were sent to Kang’s data centers.
The outlet’s attempts to reach Alice Huang and Kang Wei were not successful.

Kang’s data center business reportedly included a Shanghai-based firm called Century Longteng – in which a local Shanghai government group held a 10% stake and Kang’s main firm, Hexi Capital, held a 27% stake. Kang eventually took an executive position at Century Longteng.

paragraphs: A senior Nvidia employee sent a letter to the company’s top executives and board of directors arguing that failure to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could lead to the loss of “irreplaceable talent,” according to people familiar with the matter.

The letter, written by director of developer technology Nader Khalil, escalates an internal push to bring Huang back following his resignation on Thursday. It argues that Huang is uniquely qualified to lead Nvidia and deserves the benefit of the doubt as the board investigates his relationship with a Singapore data-center executive suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia is stuck between a rock and a hard place, as "irreplaceable talent" wants to leave if Jensen Huang isn't reinstated as CEO amidst the spy affair controversy.

Following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang, there are warnings that important Nvidia employees are planning to leave if the company doesn’t reinstate him. According to the Wall Street Journal, an employee sent an internal letter to the top executives and board of directors stating that “failure to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could lead to the loss of ‘irreplaceable talent.’” Huang resigned last week amidst a firestorm of reports about an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, a further affair with VP of health care Kimberly Powell, and allegations the former relationship may have facilitated chip smuggling into China.

According to WSJ’s sources, director of developer technology Nader Khalil wrote the letter, urging that Huang be reinstated as CEO, lest the company lose loyal and important employees. The letter’s recipients, according to WSJ, comprised roughly 60 direct reports and the 10 members of the board, and Khalil warned that “Irreplaceable talent at Nvidia is now contemplating departing.”

The internal letter, along with the standwithjensen.com open letter to reinstate him, shows how important Huang is to the employees of Nvidia. Without the key long-term employees, which the company heavily depends on, progress could halt, or possibly regress, as Nvidia would lose the employees who have worked on and built the architectures and systems that make Nvidia what it is, along with their leader, Huang — who has recently stated that he would be honored to come back as CEO.

The open letter, signed by multiple Nvidia current and former employees, and tech CEOs and investors, states that employees are concerned that Huang was ousted unfairly and without due process, expressing that the employees do not have “access to the board’s private deliberations,” and that they have not been shown evidence that Alice Huang was indeed a spy, which even US intelligence doesn’t have solid evidence of. The open letter demands that Huang be reinstated as CEO while ensuring an independent investigation and a fair hearing, including providing a “specific, evidence-based explanation” of why Nvidia shouldn’t keep Huang as CEO — with Huang scheduled to appear before a House of Foreign Affairs panel concerning his affairs with the alleged spy.

Despite the letter, the support of other Silicon Valley CEOs, and even President Trump, Nvidia is still not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Nvidia is the hottest AI hardware company at the moment, and its employees are highly desirable not only within the US, but possibly China as well. China surely wouldn’t mind getting its hands on a few key employees, who, if they choose to leave, are likely not going to have a hard time finding another job.

paragraphs: Kalshi, a pioneer in the newfangled prediction markets, is now expanding into one of Wall Street’s oldest businesses: stock trading.
The company bought FB securities, a small New York-based broker, in July and plans to launch equity trading within the next two months, people familiar with the matter said.
The prediction-market platform plans to offer stocks and ETFs within two months as it builds toward a multi-asset exchange
Mon 16 Nov 2026 · 15:23 EST · 3 min read
Kalshi built its name on letting people trade on whether things will happen. Now it wants them trading things that already exist.
The CFTC-regulated prediction-market platform plans to launch stock and ETF trading within two months. The plan follows its acquisition of FB Securities, a broker-dealer based in New York.
Kalshi acquired FB Securities in July 2026. The two-month launch window surfaced in Wall Street Journal reports dated November 16, 2026.

Counting forward from those reports, the research points to a launch that could land around mid-January 2027. That date is an estimate based on the reported window, not a confirmed launch day from the company.
The financial terms of the deal have not been disclosed. Neither Kalshi nor any other party has published a price tag for FB Securities.

The value of the purchase lies less in the brand than in the plumbing. A broker-dealer brings brokerage infrastructure and the regulatory permissions needed to let customers buy and sell stocks and ETFs directly.

For Kalshi, that shortcut matters. Its existing business runs under CFTC oversight, which covers event contracts and derivatives. Offering ordinary equities requires a different set of approvals, and owning a broker-dealer is one way to bring those approvals in-house.

Kalshi frames the move as part of a broader effort to become a multi-asset financial exchange. That lineup would combine three categories under one roof.

First come its prediction markets, the core product where users trade contracts tied to real-world outcomes. Second are perpetual futures, derivatives that let traders take positions on price moves without a set expiry date.
Third, if the plan holds, will be traditional equity products: individual stocks and exchange-traded funds. ETFs are baskets of assets that trade like a single share.
The company has the money behind that ambition. Kalshi’s Series G funding round in October 2026 valued it at approximately $40 billion.

Kalshi’s identity has been tied to prediction markets, a format that turns questions about future events into tradable contracts. Prices on those contracts move as traders update their views on how likely an outcome is.

Operating under CFTC regulation has been central to its pitch. It positions Kalshi as a regulated venue rather than an offshore betting site, a distinction that matters to users and to the institutions backing it.
The later addition of perpetual futures already pushed the platform beyond pure event trading. Stocks and ETFs extend that drift further toward the territory of established retail trading platforms.

paragraphs: Cybersecurity startup Corma raised $125 million to build automated agents that run on cyber-trained artificial-intelligence models.

Led by venture investor New Enterprise Associates, the Series A funding round comes three months after Corma emerged from stealth with $60 million in seed capital. NEA joins existing investors Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue. The latest round boosts Corma’s market valuation to $1 billion, the company said.

The same AI that is getting better at writing code is getting better at breaking it. Vulnerabilities are just another kind of bug, and agents can now exploit what they find end to end. Defense is a different problem: it means digging through audit logs, security events and network flows, correlating weak signals across systems and over long time horizons, and staying consistent across thousands of decisions in a row. Corma, a startup that trains its own foundation models for that work, has reached unicorn status three months after emerging from stealth.

Corma trains foundation models for defensive cybersecurity and deploys them as an AI workforce that works alongside enterprise security teams. A foundation model here means a base AI model trained at scale for a specific domain rather than adapted from a general-purpose one. According to Sequoia Capital, Corma trains its model with reinforcement learning on simulated enterprise networks that include their tools, telemetry and noise. The model is not a technology supplied to other security vendors. It powers Corma’s own workforce, which runs inside the security tools a customer already uses and carries out tasks from start to finish. In effect, Corma trains the model and places it with customers as AI staff. CEO Alon Pluda told Israeli outlet Calcalist, “We don’t replace anyone and we are not a product,” and said the company sells virtual human resources.

The company says coding models were never optimized for defensive work, so the progress that makes AI a better attacker barely moves defense. It is headquartered in Tel Aviv and San Francisco, and its team includes researchers from Google DeepMind and security experts from Israel’s Unit 8200.
Alon Pluda is co-founder and CEO. Sequoia Capital, which led Corma’s seed round, has described him as one of the most elite hackers in the world.

Corma announced a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation. NEA led the round, with existing investors Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue participating. It comes three months after Corma disclosed a $60 million seed led by Sequoia in August, bringing total funding to $185 million.

According to the company, demand has surged across the Fortune 100, Fortune 500 and Fortune Global 500 since it left stealth, and it has expanded server capacity 24x to keep up. It says some large enterprises already had the Corma workforce in place when “Black October,” a wave of critical vulnerabilities and breaches in widely used software, hit in October. Pluda said securing enough compute has been one of the company’s hardest problems. NEA partner Aaron Jacobson said Corma is building the intelligence layer defensive security needs, and called it the only company taking on the problem in a way that scales across organizations. Corma plans to use the new funds to scale its foundation models and compute, and said it will share its next-generation models soon.

Corma’s closest rivals are startups automating security operations with AI. 7AI raised a $130 million Series A, which it billed as the largest in cybersecurity history, led by Index Ventures. Torq raised a $140 million Series D and became a unicorn. Exaforce raised a $125 million Series B for its agentic SOC, bringing total funding to $200 million. While they ship agents and platforms that automate security operations, Corma pitches an AI workforce driven by its own model instead of software. The comparison Corma itself draws is with general-purpose frontier models, which it argues are a poor fit for defensive work.

paragraphs: | Photography by Emily Kask for WSJ
BATON ROUGE, La.—They rise early here like bees from a hive—in this case, an enormous Amazon fulfillment center.
Fans watch as the Prime Air drones dart over trees, roads and power lines before they make a beeline to customers, descend in a rush of air and drop boxes onto their lawns.

WESTBOROUGH — Stephanie Stuchlik lives about a mile from Amazon’s colossal warehouse, where dozens of blue-vested drivers haul packages every day. But at home, under a clear sky in her lush backyard, she doesn’t notice any of that action.
Soon, her reality could transform, as Amazon plans to launch a fleet of 83-pound delivery drones that would zip overhead — up to 1,000 times a day.
“It’s going to ruin our town,” said the 40-year-old mother of two, who works in real estate. “It will ruin how I use my home to the point that I would want to move, frankly.”

That science fiction-esque reality is approaching fast. Too fast, for some residents, like Stuchlik, who are chasing any way to hit the brakes on the project. Amazon wants to convert a parking lot at the Westborough Fulfillment Center into an Amazon Prime Air Drone Delivery launching pad. From there, drones would fly in and out to deliver small packages to more than a dozen cities and towns in a 7.5-mile radius that would also affect parts of Worcester and Shrewsbury.

According to Amazon, Westborough drones are all but a done deal. But on Wednesday morning, members of the state’s congressional delegation weighed in; US Senators Ed Markey and Elizabeth Warren, with Representatives Lori Trahan and Jim McGovern, sent letters to Amazon and the FAA, demanding a study to assess the impacts of drone delivery in the region. They wrote, “Amazon is now trying to quickly move drone operations into Massachusetts under a streamlined regulatory process the state itself is challenging.”
“From noise pollution to fire risks, communities have plenty of reasons to question Big Tech’s plan to fill their skies with drones,” Markey said in a statement.
The town cannot regulate the airspace, as that is FAA territory. But it does hold one card: how the site will be zoned.

Amazon first presented the 6,800-square-foot launch pad as an “accessory” to the facility, meaning it would only need the town Planning Board’s approval. John Gelcich, the board’s vice-chair, said the town cannot deny a site plan as long as it meets safety requirements.

Amazon says it wants to serve 500 communities nationwide using drones by the end of the year. It already operates about 15 drone delivery centers around the country. This would be the first drone delivery service in New England. Amazon has proposed launching drones in Connecticut, but it’s met opposition there as well. As the technology rapidly spreads nationwide, residents are left questioning what, if any, power they have to challenge Big Tech.

In late September, roughly 13 residents, including Stuchlik, formed an opposition group they call Mass Blue Skies, and filed an appeal to the Zoning Board of Appeals. The group challenges the accessory classification and argues the launching pad is technically an airport, under the town’s by-laws, and should be zoned under a special permit. This pushed Amazon’s expected project start date of October to at least early November, when the Appeals Board is slated to deliberate on the classification.

“This is an incredibly pivotal moment for Westborough, as the epicenter of a potential drone delivery expansion,” said resident Christine Farmer, 63, a founding member of Mass Blue Skies. “If Amazon launches, other companies can come in as well.”

Amazon says it’s aware of the appeal. “We are continuing to work through the required planning, reviews, and approvals,” Lindsay Hamilton, an Amazon spokesperson, said in a statement. “Community and customer feedback helps to shape how we operate, and we’ll keep listening as we move forward.”

The company landed in this suburb 30 miles west of Boston in 2021 and has often been referred to as a “good neighbor” by community members and town officials. Half a dozen residents told the Globe in interviews they’re not against Amazon; many enjoy the convenience of Prime deliveries. Their resistance to commercial delivery drones is part of something bigger — fears of a grimmer, dystopian future, in which machines clutter the sky and erase the serenity of the place they call home.
Residents voiced their concerns at an Amazon presentation about the concept last month, where hundreds of people buzzed with disdain.
“Do we want to look up in the sky and see blue sky, or do we want to see a highway of drones?” one Hopkinton resident said at the Sept. 23 meeting, posted on the town’s YouTube channel.

Tareq Wafaie, an Amazon Air representative who took questions from residents for more than two hours at the meeting, told them, “There is no opting out of drones flying over your property. That is [Federal Aviation Administration] controlled airspace.”
He said he would relay residents’ concerns about noise, safety, and privacy to the company.

For attendees, that was not enough. Some complained that opting-out of the service would not prevent neighbors from making a different choice and summoning drones. Anything under five pounds, from pet food to medical supplies or last-minute mac and cheese, could be dropped at a customer’s doorstep in under one hour — or as little as 30 minutes. (The service is optional and can be free of charge or cost up to $4.99, depending on the order price and whether a customer is a Prime member, according to the company.)

Kade Crockford, director for Technology and Justice Programs at the American Civil Liberties Union of Massachusetts, has tracked the backlash that surrounds Flock Safety, a company mired in controversy over data security concerns and misuse of its automatic license plate reader cameras.
For Crockford, the Westborough community organizing against the drones does not come as a surprise.

“People are sick and tired of having [tech] companies dictate to us what our rights will be and what our lives will look like,” she said. “People don’t just want to be acted upon by the wealthiest men in the world. They want to have power over their own lives.”

The FAA issued a ruling this summer that it found “no significant” environmental impact from package deliveries by drones after a study conducted in 23 states — none in New England. Massachusetts is one of 15 states suing the FAA over the nationwide decision.
The four members of Congress argue the agency and Amazon have bypassed site-specific study requirements, and demand a response by Oct. 29.

“As new drone operations expand, operators and local community leaders have primary responsibility for raising awareness and addressing community concerns regarding those operations,” an FAA spokesperson said in a statement, adding that the agency’s role is to ensure compliance with safety and federal regulations.

Mass Blue Skies surveyed community members to gauge response to the delivery center. Out of more than 1,500 responses, 92 percent said they oppose it, with noise and residential overflights being the top concerns. Amazon says fewer than 1 percent of customer service inquiries it receives are about noise. It compares the noise to that of a passing car.

In other parts of the country, residents took action too late. In Texas, Brian Rowe offered a cautionary tale, as a drone zoomed overhead during an interview with the Globe. “One just flew past my house,” he said from Richardson, a Dallas suburb.

Richardson’s City Council approved Amazon’s drones last year, and Walmart’s fleet also flies above, generating a gentle but constant buzz throughout the day. He likened the sound to a lawnmower in a neighbor’s yard — only the drones’ whirring goes on all day, until nightfall.
Rowe, a tech and cybersecurity executive, lives about half a mile from the city’s Amazon warehouse, and at any given moment, he said, he can see or hear a drone.

“What’s the impact to the quality of life of my children growing up in a space where there’s a constant drone overhead?” he said. ”I see a future where the air is just full of this mess, and we’ve done nothing to think about the implications or the impact it has."
He offered a warning to Massachusetts residents: “You better make your voice heard before it becomes a reality,” he said. “It’s easier to stop it than undo it.”
Not everyone is displeased with the drones. Some people have recorded videos of their first deliveries and posted them on social media to songs such as Ariana Grande’s “Just Like Magic.”

A handful of videos have captured incidents like a drone hitting an apartment building or dropping a package into a swimming pool. Amazon says such misfires are “extremely rare,” and that drones use cameras and sensors for navigation. The videos and data captured are stored on encrypted drives and can only be accessed by authorized workers, per Amazon. The company says the stored data is used only for “safety purposes and to improve the customer experience.”

Versions of a consumer data privacy bill passed by the state Senate and the House could address some of the privacy and surveillance concerns raised by residents; the measure is currently in reconciliation.
Meanwhile, Westborough residents continue to raise the alarm over this, demanding Amazon listen to their concerns.
“We need to look at Amazon as a wonderful neighbor as they’ve been,” Farmer said. But for this project, “The people have spoken. They don’t want this.”

WESTBOROUGH — Stephanie Stuchlik lives about a mile from Amazon’s colossal warehouse, where dozens of blue-vested drivers haul packages every day. But at home, under a clear sky in her lush backyard, she doesn’t notice any of that action.

Soon, her reality could transform, as Amazon plans to launch a fleet of 83-pound delivery drones that would zip overhead — up to 1,000 times a day.

“It’s going to ruin our town,” said the 40-year-old mother of two, who works in real estate. “It will ruin how I use my home to the point that I would want to move, frankly.”

That science fiction-esque reality is approaching fast. Too fast, for some residents, like Stuchlik, who are chasing any way to hit the brakes on the project. Amazon wants to convert a parking lot at the Westborough Fulfillment Center into an Amazon Prime Air Drone Delivery launching pad. From there, drones would fly in and out to deliver small packages to more than a dozen cities and towns in a 7.5-mile radius that would also affect parts of Worcester and Shrewsbury.

According to Amazon, Westborough drones are all but a done deal. But on Wednesday morning, members of the state’s congressional delegation weighed in; US Senators Ed Markey and Elizabeth Warren, with Representatives Lori Trahan and Jim McGovern, sent letters to Amazon and the FAA, demanding a study to assess the impacts of drone delivery in the region. They wrote, “Amazon is now trying to quickly move drone operations into Massachusetts under a streamlined regulatory process the state itself is challenging.”

“From noise pollution to fire risks, communities have plenty of reasons to question Big Tech’s plan to fill their skies with drones,” Markey said in a statement.

The town cannot regulate the airspace, as that is FAA territory. But it does hold one card: how the site will be zoned.

Amazon first presented the 6,800-square-foot launch pad as an “accessory” to the facility, meaning it would only need the town Planning Board’s approval. John Gelcich, the board’s vice-chair, said the town cannot deny a site plan as long as it meets safety requirements.

Amazon says it wants to serve 500 communities nationwide using drones by the end of the year. It already operates about 15 drone delivery centers around the country. This would be the first drone delivery service in New England. Amazon has proposed launching drones in Connecticut, but it’s met opposition there as well. As the technology rapidly spreads nationwide, residents are left questioning what, if any, power they have to challenge Big Tech.

In late September, roughly 13 residents, including Stuchlik, formed an opposition group they call Mass Blue Skies, and filed an appeal to the Zoning Board of Appeals. The group challenges the accessory classification and argues the launching pad is technically an airport, under the town’s by-laws, and should be zoned under a special permit. This pushed Amazon’s expected project start date of October to at least early November, when the Appeals Board is slated to deliberate on the classification.

“This is an incredibly pivotal moment for Westborough, as the epicenter of a potential drone delivery expansion,” said resident Christine Farmer, 63, a founding member of Mass Blue Skies. “If Amazon launches, other companies can come in as well.”

Amazon says it’s aware of the appeal. “We are continuing to work through the required planning, reviews, and approvals,” Lindsay Hamilton, an Amazon spokesperson, said in a statement. “Community and customer feedback helps to shape how we operate, and we’ll keep listening as we move forward.”

The company landed in this suburb 30 miles west of Boston in 2021 and has often been referred to as a “good neighbor” by community members and town officials. Half a dozen residents told the Globe in interviews they’re not against Amazon; many enjoy the convenience of Prime deliveries. Their resistance to commercial delivery drones is part of something bigger — fears of a grimmer, dystopian future, in which machines clutter the sky and erase the serenity of the place they call home.

Residents voiced their concerns at an Amazon presentation about the concept last month, where hundreds of people buzzed with disdain.

“Do we want to look up in the sky and see blue sky, or do we want to see a highway of drones?” one Hopkinton resident said at the Sept. 23 meeting, posted on the town’s YouTube channel.

Tareq Wafaie, an Amazon Air representative who took questions from residents for more than two hours at the meeting, told them, “There is no opting out of drones flying over your property. That is [Federal Aviation Administration] controlled airspace.”

He said he would relay residents’ concerns about noise, safety, and privacy to the company.

For attendees, that was not enough. Some complained that opting-out of the service would not prevent neighbors from making a different choice and summoning drones. Anything under five pounds, from pet food to medical supplies or last-minute mac and cheese, could be dropped at a customer’s doorstep in under one hour — or as little as 30 minutes. (The service is optional and can be free of charge or cost up to $4.99, depending on the order price and whether a customer is a Prime member, according to the company.)

Kade Crockford, director for Technology and Justice Programs at the American Civil Liberties Union of Massachusetts, has tracked the backlash that surrounds Flock Safety, a company mired in controversy over data security concerns and misuse of its automatic license plate reader cameras.

For Crockford, the Westborough community organizing against the drones does not come as a surprise.

“People are sick and tired of having [tech] companies dictate to us what our rights will be and what our lives will look like,” she said. “People don’t just want to be acted upon by the wealthiest men in the world. They want to have power over their own lives.”

The FAA issued a ruling this summer that it found “no significant” environmental impact from package deliveries by drones after a study conducted in 23 states — none in New England. Massachusetts is one of 15 states suing the FAA over the nationwide decision.

The four members of Congress argue the agency and Amazon have bypassed site-specific study requirements, and demand a response by Oct. 29.

“As new drone operations expand, operators and local community leaders have primary responsibility for raising awareness and addressing community concerns regarding those operations,” an FAA spokesperson said in a statement, adding that the agency’s role is to ensure compliance with safety and federal regulations.

Mass Blue Skies surveyed community members to gauge response to the delivery center. Out of more than 1,500 responses, 92 percent said they oppose it, with noise and residential overflights being the top concerns. Amazon says fewer than 1 percent of customer service inquiries it receives are about noise. It compares the noise to that of a passing car.

In other parts of the country, residents took action too late. In Texas, Brian Rowe offered a cautionary tale, as a drone zoomed overhead during an interview with the Globe. “One just flew past my house,” he said from Richardson, a Dallas suburb.

Richardson’s City Council approved Amazon’s drones last year, and Walmart’s fleet also flies above, generating a gentle but constant buzz throughout the day. He likened the sound to a lawnmower in a neighbor’s yard — only the drones’ whirring goes on all day, until nightfall.

Rowe, a tech and cybersecurity executive, lives about half a mile from the city’s Amazon warehouse, and at any given moment, he said, he can see or hear a drone.

“What’s the impact to the quality of life of my children growing up in a space where there’s a constant drone overhead?” he said. ”I see a future where the air is just full of this mess, and we’ve done nothing to think about the implications or the impact it has."

He offered a warning to Massachusetts residents: “You better make your voice heard before it becomes a reality,” he said. “It’s easier to stop it than undo it.”

Not everyone is displeased with the drones. Some people have recorded videos of their first deliveries and posted them on social media to songs such as Ariana Grande’s “Just Like Magic.”

A handful of videos have captured incidents like a drone hitting an apartment building or dropping a package into a swimming pool. Amazon says such misfires are “extremely rare,” and that drones use cameras and sensors for navigation. The videos and data captured are stored on encrypted drives and can only be accessed by authorized workers, per Amazon. The company says the stored data is used only for “safety purposes and to improve the customer experience.”

Versions of a consumer data privacy bill passed by the state Senate and the House could address some of the privacy and surveillance concerns raised by residents; the measure is currently in reconciliation.

Meanwhile, Westborough residents continue to raise the alarm over this, demanding Amazon listen to their concerns.

“We need to look at Amazon as a wonderful neighbor as they’ve been,” Farmer said. But for this project, “The people have spoken. They don’t want this.”

paragraphs: Data centers on land have attracted a lot of opposition. So in response, more companies have an alternative: What if data centers were placed on the ocean, or on some other body of water, instead?

The idea is still in the early stages. But as battles over where to build data centers intensify, developers are betting that offshore facilities could face less opposition from the public. They wouldn’t be located in neighborhoods, and many of the proposed projects plan to generate electricity from waves or tidal power and use seawater for cooling, which could help alleviate fears about power and water consumption.

The artificial intelligence boom is driving unprecedented demand for data centers, raising concerns about their growing energy consumption, water use and carbon footprint. These challenges are making companies look beyond traditional land-based data centers.

Some developers are now exploring the ocean as a new location for AI infrastructure in the hopes that underwater data centers could improve energy use and cooling efficiency while using less fresh water and land area than onshore buildings.

My research focuses on the societal, organizational and environmental implications of emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence and the digital infrastructure – including data centers – that supports its development and deployment. I see underwater data centers as a promising new approach for supporting the growth of AI.

But moving servers into the ocean does not make other underlying environmental challenges such as energy consumption and carbon emissions disappear. And it creates new concerns about harm to the marine environment, as well as questions about how these data centers can be regulated – and how companies can maintain and expand them if needed. Whether underwater data centers can become sustainable alternatives to traditional data centers depends on solving these economic, technical and environmental problems.
An underwater data center is under construction in a Chinese shipyard in September 2025. CN-STR / AFP via Getty Images

In 2015, Microsoft launched a research project to explore the feasibility, benefits and challenges of underwater data centers. Part of that effort included setting up a waterproof data center on the seafloor near Scotland's Orkney Islands in 2018. It contained 864 servers and was connected to shore by an underwater cable.

After two years, Microsoft reported that the servers in the underwater data center failed at about one-eighth the rate of servers in comparable land-based data centers. The company is still studying the possible reasons but hypothesizes that in a sealed underwater environment the equipment is less exposed to oxygen, humidity and temperature fluctuations – as well as less jostling from people working to replace broken components.

However, Microsoft ended the project in 2024 and chose not to build more underwater data centers. The company didn't say why, but others' analyses suggest the reasons could include regulatory concerns, including the need for environmental permits, as well as a desire for faster upgrades and replacements for the computer equipment inside.
Instead the company has focused on land-based data centers, which can be larger and easier to expand, and also easier to access to repair or replace equipment.

Others have moved ahead, though. China built what may be the world's first wind-powered underwater data center in Shanghai. The facility launched in June 2025 and began full commercial operations in May 2026.

The US$226 million project uses seawater as a coolant rather than have to refrigerate fresh water, reducing the electricity required to cool the computers. It uses at least 30% less electricity than traditional data centers, and offshore wind turbines reduce reliance on fossil fuels and cut the data center's carbon emissions.

Japan is testing a different approach: Data centers housed in containers on floating platforms at sea can use seawater for cooling, have unobstructed conditions for solar panels and wind turbines, and reduce demand for land. In 2025, a data center in shipping containers opened on a floating platform near Yokohama. Its power comes from solar panels installed on the same floating platform, with batteries providing energy storage. The test will continue through March 2027.

Singapore is also moving toward commercial-scale floating data centers. In 2026, infrastructure company Keppel began building a four-story floating data center, scheduled to open in 2028. The project will use seawater for cooling, reducing reliance on treated water and improving cooling efficiency. And the fact that it floats means it won't take up any of Singapore's limited land availability.
In 2025, Ulsan, South Korea, began planning an underwater data center that could house more than 100,000 servers and use 30% less power than land-based centers by using seawater for cooling.
In Maine, DeepGreen Western Passage has proposed a submersible AI data center in the Bay of Fundy, powered by tidal turbines designed to harness the area's strong tidal currents.

Land-based data centers could also take advantage of seawater cooling. In Portugal, the SIN01 AI data center in Sines uses seawater from the Atlantic to cool its servers before returning it to the ocean.
An artist's depiction of a floating data center in Yokohama, Japan. Yokohama City Government via Japan News
These various approaches offer ways to reduce demand for grid-supplied electricity for powering data centers' computers and cooling equipment, as well as using less fresh water.

The distance from people's homes could also be an advantage for data centers in or on the ocean. A Gallup poll in March 2026 found that 70% of Americans oppose building AI data centers in their communities. However, more than half of the world's population lives within 120 miles of a coast. Underwater could be another way to keep data centers physically close to users for speedy service.

Maintenance, though, is a major challenge. If a computer fails underwater, it cannot be repaired or replaced on site. The entire sealed data center module may need to be brought to the surface, even if just one computer needs work.
Land-based data centers are easier to maintain and expand than floating or underwater data centers. Yasuyoshi Chiba / AFP via Getty Images

The main environmental concern about ocean-based data centers involves the seawater used for cooling. Discharging warm or hot water can potentially affect oxygen levels, pH and marine life in the surrounding waters.

That heat is already apparent at the few seaborne data centers now operating. HiCloud, the engineering contractor for China's Hainan underwater data center, has reported a temperature increase of less than 1 degree Celsius (1.8 degrees Fahrenheit) in the seawater near the facility. SIN01 in Sines, Portugal, also returns seawater about 1 C warmer.

Many marine species depend on stable water temperatures for breeding, feeding and migration, raising concerns that heat released by multiple underwater data centers could create localized thermal pollution and alter marine ecosystems. And the ocean is already under pressure. UNESCO, the United Nations agency for international cooperation, including in conservation, estimates that about 60% of marine ecosystems are already degraded or used unsustainably.

The ocean is already warming along with the atmosphere, without additional waste heat from data centers. paragraphs: Nvidia will be one of more than two dozen companies designated artificial intelligence “national champions” as part of an effort by the Trump administration to help AI firms win business overseas, people familiar with the plans said.

The announcement, which is expected within the next week, indicates the administration is barreling ahead with its tech strategy despite the turmoil surrounding Nvidia. The national champions initiative is part of an effort to get foreign companies and countries to adopt U.S. AI technology over Chinese rivals.

The Trump administration is preparing to designate Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, OpenAI and Anthropic, among more than two dozen American companies, as artificial intelligence “national champions”, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal. The proposed initiative is aimed at helping US technology firms expand overseas and compete with Chinese rivals in the global AI market.
A formal announcement is expected within the coming week, with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick likely to lead it, the report said. The timeline, however, could change.

The programme seeks to encourage foreign governments and businesses to adopt American-developed AI systems instead of Chinese alternatives. It would bring together US-made processors, AI architectures and related products in packages intended to make procurement easier for overseas buyers.
Portraits of Dreamers and Doers under 35

Companies selected under the initiative could receive faster authorisations for export licences, government support for international operations and access to federal funding mechanisms, according to details on the Commerce Department's initiative portal.
First unveiled around a year ago as part of the administration's broader technology strategy, the programme's list of participating companies had not previously been made public.

The initiative reflects Washington's efforts to strengthen the international presence of American AI companies as competition with Beijing intensifies. Chinese firms, including Huawei Technologies, have been expanding their presence in markets across Europe and Latin America.

Nvidia's expected inclusion comes amid continuing debate in Washington over the export of advanced AI chips to China. Its processors power many of the world's most sophisticated AI systems and are central to the development of advanced computing infrastructure.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly praised Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang, for building a major American technology company at the centre of the AI boom.

But the company's role in the global chip market has also placed it under scrutiny from national security officials and lawmakers concerned that advanced Nvidia components could reach Chinese entities through gaps in export controls.

The Wall Street Journal report said disclosures concerning Huang's alleged links to a Chinese intelligence operative have added to pressure from critics calling for national security considerations to take precedence over commercial interests.

Lutnick has also faced criticism over claims that the Commerce Department has not adequately closed loopholes that could allow Chinese companies to obtain advanced Nvidia chips. The Wall Street Journal has previously reported concerns about his reluctance to alienate Beijing during trade negotiations.

The planned announcement comes as Lutnick prepares to accompany Trump on a diplomatic visit to China this week. The Commerce Department is also expected to advance new regulations to prevent the illicit diversion of high-performance processors to Beijing.

Expanding American AI exports has been a central part of the Trump administration's technology agenda since last summer. Washington views the initiative as a way to secure overseas markets for US-developed systems and reinforce its position in a sector increasingly shaped by strategic competition with China.
The proposed national champions framework would combine technology, export facilitation and diplomatic support in an effort to make American AI products more accessible to foreign buyers.

paragraphs: In his final months as chief executive of Nvidia, Jensen Huang was laying the groundwork to pull back the company’s approach to backstopping the AI economy.
Now, with a finance chief at the helm who was already wary of some deals the ousted chief forged, the startups who had been counting on Nvidia’s support expect an even greater pullback.
Just last month, the CEOs of emerging cloud companies that buy Nvidia chips and rent out computing power gathered in Berlin

Huang told his partners that if their companies wanted allocations of Nvidia’s prized GPUs, they would need to secure upfront payments from customers, people in attendance said. That would make their projects easier to finance and ensure that Nvidia wasn’t alone in being a source of financial support.

“You’re not charging what you should be charging,” he said, telling them that Elon Musk was renting Nvidia chips to customers at better rates than they were. “I don’t even need you guys. I could just give all this capacity to Elon! Elon wants it!” he said, according to two executives who heard the remarks and one who was briefed on them shortly after.

Weeks later, Huang resigned after revelations that he had engaged in at least two affairs, including one with a woman U.S. officials believe is a Chinese intelligence asset and another with one of his direct reports. His interim successor, finance chief Colette Kress, has at times pushed back against some of the company’s big deals and sought to rein in Nvidia.
Many companies that had relied on Nvidia are now worried.
UBS analyst Tim Arcuri estimated in a recent note that an Nvidia financing pullback could take $50 billion or more out of the market, starving companies of support as interest rates rise.

The chip giant spent much of the past year on a dealmaking spree to provide financial backstops to emerging companies, lend its balance sheet to support debt financings of data-center projects, and even act as a customer of last resort for its own chips. The firm agreed to rent its chips from some customers to signal to lenders that those companies had solid contracts in-hand.
Earlier this year, Nvidia signaled it was preparing to roll out new financial incentives and do more deals than ever.

Rivals, such as Alphabet’s Google and Advanced Micro Devices, were offering these companies similar incentives, and Huang didn’t want to lose market share. Among the executives leading the charge was Nico Caprez, an Nvidia vice president who is also Huang’s son-in-law.
Nvidia announced its financing program in July, but by August, Huang and Kress questioned the return on investment from some deals.

When Nvidia used its creditworthy balance sheet to help OpenAI sign a massive data center lease in Piketon, Ohio, with SoftBank’s SB Energy, it cut the scale of its commitment in August during negotiations. Kress had become skeptical of the scale of the deal.

Huang told his finance team in August that the company was under pressure, The Wall Street Journal previously reported. Major cloud providers were making plans to use alternative chips and lessen their reliance on the firm, and Nvidia was staring at a glut of chip wafers and memory it had committed to buying, he told them.
The then-CEO pressed staff to develop a way to decide whether guarantees were worthwhile. Later that month, it paused some deals in that initiative, the Journal reported.
U.K.-based neocloud Nscale is still negotiating with Nvidia and other investors to provide financial backing for a $45-billion data center for Anthropic in West Virginia, the Journal reported.

In addition to its extensive backstopping, the chip maker also made a string of equity investments in AI startups. In total, Nvidia has participated in a record 129 venture-capital deals this year, as of Nov. 10, accounting for 27% of global VC deal value, according to PitchBook, up from a total of 49 such deals in 2023.
CEOs of startups that had closed deals with Nvidia breathed a sigh of relief that their deals made it through before Huang’s ouster.

Perplexity Chief Executive Aravind Srinivas shared that Nvidia closed a $3 billion investment in the company with his employees during a weekly all-hands at the startup’s San Francisco headquarters on Oct. 30, a person familiar with the meeting said. It was one day after news broke that the Nvidia CEO was seen as a target of a Chinese spy plot.
The AI search company is now raising additional capital at a higher valuation of $38 billion before the new investment, according to people familiar with the matter.

Nvidia recently made an offer to Reflection AI, an open-source model developer valued at $25 billion, to license its technology and hire away some of its talent, according to people familiar with the matter. Huang had publicly praised the company. An agreement hadn’t been reached before he left, the people said.

Nvidia has also been finalizing a massive investment in Thinking Machines Lab, another provider of open-source models, valuing the company at $40 billion, according to people familiar with the matter. Thinking Machines is confident the deal will be completed, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Some details of Nvidia’s recent investments were earlier reported by the Financial Times and The Information.

Reflection and Thinking Machines are burning huge amounts of capital each month to pay for the computing power to develop their AI models, but haven’t yet developed a way to generate substantial revenue.

Some founders and venture-capital backers of companies with little to no sales said that if Nvidia did pull back from future equity investments, they could struggle to find capital to keep their cash-hungry businesses going, let alone secure a lucrative exit.

paragraphs: SENAWANG, Malaysia—An hour outside of the Malaysian capital, Bangladeshi workers this past week were driving dump trucks and excavators at a site stretching across 117 football fields.

It was a world away from the Silicon Valley boardroom where, hours later, Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang would be ousted. Yet this site in Southeast Asia and others like it are at the heart of the Huang affair.

Here, a Chinese company plans to use Nvidia’s advanced artificial-intelligence chips. Thanks to Chinese customers, data-center industry leaders say Malaysia could become the second-largest data center hub in the world, after Virginia, packed with top-of-the-line Nvidia chips China’s leading AI companies can use to challenge American dominance.

Huang built a multibillion-dollar business to feed the ravenous appetite of Chinese customers for American chips, cultivating a network of Asian partners who could serve the Chinese far from Washington. He made a friend of President Trump and lobbied Washington hard to keep the backdoor to China open.
Kang Wei’s investment firm owned a 27 percent stake in a data center developer, while his wife gained access to Nvidia’s chip supply chain.

The husband of Alice Huang — a woman accused of being a Chinese spy and having an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — has reportedly pursued a massive data center project backed by the Chinese government.

Kang Wei, Alice Huang's husband, had planned more than $9 billion in data center investments from 2021 through 2024, the Wall Street Journal reported Monday after examining Chinese corporate disclosures and official government statements.
Long before the alleged affair, Kang and the Nvidia founder had become acquainted through the video game business. Kang reportedly set up an introduction to his wife himself.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Kang appeared to have quietly acquiesced to the relationship between his wife and Jensen Huang, according to acquaintances of the couple.
Kang's foray into the data center project began in late 2021, ahead of Washington's move to curb shipments of cutting-edge AI semiconductors to China.

The venture revolved around Century Longteng, a data center developer headquartered in Shanghai. At the time, the Chinese gaming company Century Huatong was its largest shareholder with a 63 percent stake. A Kang-linked investment firm owned 27 percent, and an agency under the Shanghai city government held the other 10 percent.
Huawei, the Chinese telecom equipment maker targeted by U.S. sanctions, agreed with Century Longteng in early 2022 to jointly develop cloud data centers and computing facilities.

Century Longteng announced a $4.5 billion investment in data center construction in Wuhu, a city in Anhui Province, in the summer of 2022. The project received state backing for electricity and infrastructure as part of Beijing's push to expand computing capacity. By April this year, at least one data center building had been officially registered as complete.

Kang also attended a groundbreaking ceremony for a $5 billion data center project in Liangshan, Sichuan Province, in July 2024. He was also reportedly involved in similar ventures in Shenzhen, a major technology hub in southern China.
As her husband expanded his data center business across China, Alice Huang gained access to Nvidia's chip supply chain through the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed.
Singaporean authorities reportedly identified Alice Huang as Megaspeed’s CEO and one of its key controllers at the time.

The company secured cloud partner status with Nvidia in November 2023 after presenting Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba as a major customer. Some of the Nvidia chips the company obtained reportedly made their way into China.

The Wall Street Journal cautioned that there was no confirmation that Alice Huang had acquired Nvidia chips on orders from Chinese authorities or that the semiconductors had ended up in Kang's data center projects.

At least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia processors reached China through Alice Huang, who reportedly leveraged her personal ties to Jensen Huang, U.S. technology outlet The Information previously reported.
Authorities in the United States and Singapore are investigating Megaspeed over suspected violations of chip export controls.

The company, on its part, has maintained that its operations were lawful and that Alice Huang no longer held any position at the company. The Wall Street Journal said it had sought comment from both Kang and Alice Huang but received no response.

https://www.wsj.com/finance/corporate-ca.author: Kate Clark
paragraphs: Fintech company is reportedly seeking at least $1 billion after doubling annualized revenue to $2 billion.

Ramp, the fast-growing corporate-card and financial-management technology company, is in preliminary discussions to raise at least $1 billion at a valuation exceeding $70 billion, potentially marking its third financing round in a year.

The proposed investment would further increase Ramp’s valuation, which has more than doubled over the past 12 months as businesses increasingly adopt its financial software and artificial intelligence tools.

Existing investors Coatue Management and Thrive Capital, founded by Josh Kushner, are reportedly discussing leading the financing, according to The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the negotiations.
Founded in 2019 and led by CEO Eric Glyman, Ramp has rapidly emerged as one of the most valuable privately held financial technology companies.
In October, the company announced that its annualized revenue had surpassed $2 billion, roughly double what it was a year earlier.
Ramp also completed a $1.85 billion financing round last month at a $60 billion valuation. A new round exceeding $70 billion would represent at least a 16.7% increase in just weeks.
The company’s corporate-card business still generates most of its revenue, but its broader financial-management platform is becoming an increasingly important growth driver.
Ramp expects revenue from other services, including bill payments and banking, to surpass its corporate-card revenue within the next year.
AI Spending Creates New Growth Opportunities
Artificial intelligence has become a key part of Ramp’s expansion strategy.
The company is benefiting from rising corporate spending on AI services while developing tools that help businesses monitor and control those expenses.
Its Router product, for example, helps companies manage AI-related expenditures, addressing a growing challenge as enterprises deploy multiple AI models, applications and subscription services.

The expansion reflects Ramp’s strategy of evolving beyond corporate credit cards into a comprehensive financial-management platform that combines payments, expense controls, automation and AI-powered software.
Acquisition Strategy and Potential IPO
Ramp is expected to use part of the proceeds from its proposed financing to pursue mergers and acquisitions, potentially expanding its product offerings and market reach.
The company could pursue an initial public offering as early as 2027, although no formal timetable has been established.
Investors are closely monitoring the market for technology IPOs, including Anthropic’s anticipated public offering, as a potential indicator of investor demand for high-growth technology companies.
Ramp’s existing investor base includes Thrive Capital, Coatue Management, D1 Capital Partners, Founders Fund and Redpoint Ventures.
At a valuation exceeding $70 billion, Ramp would further strengthen its position among the world’s most valuable privately held technology companies.
The proposed transaction remains in preliminary discussions, and its final size, valuation and participating investors could change.

paragraphs: Revenue increased 10% to RMB271.519 billion ($40.498 billion), according to the company’s earnings release. Non-GAAP net income rose 92% to RMB19.909 billion, while adjusted diluted earnings per American depositary share increased 86% to RMB8.10 ($1.21). Each ADS represents eight ordinary shares.

The stock traded at $83.00, down $1.37, or 1.62%, in a premarket quotation timestamped 6:54 a.m. EST on November 19, 2026. Its November 18 closing price was $84.37 at 4 p.m. EST. Research and market data were checked at 7:04 a.m. EST; premarket prices can move sharply in thinner trading.

Reuters reported that revenue exceeded an LSEG consensus of RMB269.81 billion, but adjusted earnings per ADS missed expectations of RMB11.16. The mixed result helps explain why faster cloud growth did not immediately lift the shares.
Reported net income attributable to ordinary shareholders rose 207% to RMB64.535 billion, benefiting from investment gains excluded from adjusted earnings.

AI Cloud and Compute Services revenue increased 53% to RMB60.973 billion. External-customer recurring revenue grew 67%, excluding compute-equipment solutions. The segment’s adjusted earnings before interest, tax and amortisation increased 121% to RMB8.838 billion, with a 14.5% margin.

That improvement did not cover the losses in a separate AI business. AI Labs and Applications recorded an adjusted EBITA loss of RMB10.503 billion, against RMB3.435 billion a year earlier. Revenue in that unit increased 51% to RMB4.435 billion, but investment in AI capabilities and higher Qwen application inference costs weighed on profitability.

Capital expenditure reached RMB50.477 billion. Operating cash flow increased 55% to RMB15.690 billion, yet company-defined free cash flow deteriorated to an outflow of RMB34.472 billion from RMB21.840 billion. Over six months, free-cash outflow totalled RMB79.142 billion.

Alibaba retained RMB487.929 billion in cash and other liquid investments at September 30. Its balance-sheet bank borrowings and listed categories of notes and exchangeable bonds totalled a calculated RMB267.209 billion. The broad liquidity measure includes treasury investments; it is larger than cash alone.

Financing also carries a shareholder cost. The company raised net proceeds of HK$80 billion through new shares during the half year. Quarterly weighted-average diluted ordinary shares used for non-GAAP earnings increased to 19,777 million from 19,168 million, showing dilution alongside the investment programme.

The commerce picture remained uneven. China e-commerce revenue declined 5%, although customer-management revenue would have risen 1% excluding a subsidy-related accounting effect. International e-commerce revenue fell 8%, partly because EU customs reforms affected AliExpress. Alibaba E-commerce Group’s adjusted EBITA nevertheless increased 243%, helped by improved quick-commerce operations.

Broker targets remain much higher than the share price. Dated records show Goldman Sachs at Buy/$177 on November 19, Bernstein at a provider-normalised Buy/$165 on November 18, Bank of America at Buy/$178 on November 11, and Mizuho at a provider-normalised Buy/$200 on November 3.

Earlier assessments include J.P. Morgan’s Overweight/$200 on October 12, Jefferies’ Buy/$192 on October 8 and UBS’s Buy/$206 on September 22. Most predate these results; Goldman’s same-day entry does not establish whether its assessment followed the release.

Alibaba’s stronger cloud economics are offset by AI development losses and negative free cash flow. Its published trailing earnings multiple of 19.26 compares with 18.99 at fiscal 2026 year-end and JD.com’s (Nasdaq:JD) 15.23. Investment gains, different business models and database timing limit those comparisons.

Over the next 12 months, monitor external cloud growth, AI spending relative to cash generation, and commerce profitability. Slower cloud demand, persistent application losses or further dilutive financing without better cash returns would weaken the recovery case.

https://www.wsj.com/business/earnings/te.author: Wall Street Journal
paragraphs: Published on 11/19/2026 at 07:43 am EST
The Chinese owner of bargain-shopping app Temu posted flat earnings as it continued to deal with subdued consumer sentiment at home and regulatory pressures abroad.

Still, the results ended a string of profit declines for PDD Holdings, whose profitability has been under pressure in recent quarters it strengthens its e-commerce ecosystem. The company has also faced challenges in overseas markets amid tightened regulatory requirements and geopolitical tensions.

The company behind Temu and Chinese platform Pinduoduo on Thursday said net profit edged 0.7% higher from a year earlier to 29.54 billion yuan, equivalent to $4.43 billion. Revenue was little changed at 108.34 billion yuan.
Analysts had expected net profit of 24.81 billion yuan on revenue of 115.67 billion yuan, according to a FactSet consensus.
"We remain in a strategic investment phase, focused on strengthening supply-chain capabilities and supporting our merchants," said Jun Liu, vice president of finance.

PDD's American depositary receipts rose nearly 9% premarket, pointing to brightening investor sentiment. Appetite for the Nasdaq-listed company has waned as sentiment on tech companies weakened, leaving PDD's stock down by about one third this year.

Citi analysts pointed to Temu's shrinking user base, with Europe leading the decline as PDD faces tighter regulations in the bloc. Temu's global monthly active users fell 17.8% on iOS and 11.2% on Android in September, Citi said, citing third-party estimates.

Adding to its headwinds, the European Commission earlier this week said measures Temu put in place to tackle illegal products sold on its platform were insufficient, including what it called a "weak" content moderation system and ineffective sanctions. A PDD spokesperson said the company disagrees with the commission's view and will respond to the findings.

Meanwhile, back home, subdued consumer sentiment is weighing on Pinduoduo's performance. Total retail sales of consumer goods grew just 1.1% during the first nine months of 2026, official data showed. Sales for this year's Singles' Day--China's biggest online-shopping event of the year--rose 4.8% from last year, according to data provider Syntun.

paragraphs: Food delivery startup Wonder is moving closer to becoming a publicly traded company after confidentially filing for an initial public offering (IPO). The company announced the filing on Thursday, marking a major milestone following years of fundraising, acquisitions, and expansion.
Wonder has yet to reveal how many shares it plans to make available or the expected price range.

Founded in 2018 by entrepreneur Marc Lore, Wonder has evolved from a food delivery concept into a broader food technology business. Its model goes beyond traditional delivery apps, with the company operating food hall-style locations where customers can order meals from multiple restaurant brands through a single platform. The company handles everything from meal preparation to delivery, pickup, and dine-in service.

Lore, who previously founded Jet.com and Diapers.com, has made no secret of his plans to take Wonder public. Those ambitions gained further attention in July, when the company announced it had raised more than $650 million in a funding round that valued it at around $9 billion. Investors include Accel, GV, AllianceBernstein, and ARK Invest.

Meanwhile, Wonder has been busy expanding its footprint and strengthening its business through acquisitions. The company has outlined ambitious growth plans, including a major push into Texas, where it aims to open more than 100 locations by the end of 2027.

Additionally, Wonder has acquired meal-kit company Blue Apron, restaurant delivery platform Grubhub, media company Tastemade, and kitchen robotics company Spyce. The latter acquisition gives Wonder access to automation technology that could help streamline food preparation and improve how food is served.

Wonder is also branching out with Wonder Create, its platform focused on letting food entrepreneurs and social media influencers develop new food concepts, restaurant brands, and menu items. The platform leverages AI to design and launch restaurant brands in less than a minute.
Another notable move is its $425 million partnership with DoorDash to expand its campus dining business, which operates at 450 colleges and universities and other locations.

Despite its growth, a move into the public markets will bring new challenges. Wonder is operating in an increasingly competitive food delivery landscape, going up against established names such as DoorDash and Uber Eats.
